A band of vandals broke into
George Mason Junior-senior
High School early yesterday
causing about $4,000 damage"
and leaving the Falls Church
school q shambles.


Principal Wylie Russell termed
the carnage "the worst act Of
vandalism / have ever seen"


The group. thought to be teen
ayers, entered the school some
time after 1880 am. oy smash
ing a pane in a rear door.
George Mason earlier in the
evening lost a basketball game
to a Manassas high school out
Mr.. Russell discounted the idea
that students from the visiting
school were responsible.


Our relations with the school
have been always good. besides.
we lost" he added.


Use Hammers


After getting into the school,
the vandals lost no time. They
went into the shop and armed
themselves with hammers and
chisels.


They damaged lathes and cleo
trio saws. threw paint on the
walls and ceiling. overturned
work benches. and smashed light
fixtures.


Two porcelain drinking foun-
tains were smashed and an
empty cash register in the cafe
terra was wrecked. The front Of
the wooden service counter was
ripped off.


Fire extinguishers were emp
tied on the gym floor.


Next they turned their atten-
ton to the schools administra-
tive Office, leaving untouched the
entire east wing Of the school,
which was readily accessible.


$50 in Cash Stolen


About $50 in bills was taken
from cash boxes but $40 in
change was left. The school safe.
which contained student records
among other things, could not
be opened.


Thwarted in their efforts to
get into the principals ONCE.
the vandals wrecked havoc in
other school rooms.


Book cases. papers, vases, light
bulbs. windows were smashed
and scattered.

BONN, Germany, March / (P.
The Western Big Three and
West Germany opened negotia-
tions today on the thorny issue
of German financial support for
Western troops in this country.


Western officials predicted at
least two weeks of hard bar
gaining would follow before any
agreement could be reached.
J The American. British and
French ambassadors met in the
first sessiouat the West German
foreign Office with Deputy For
eign Minister Walter Hallstein.


Lower-level experts will take
over the negotiations tomorrow.


The United States. Britain
and France insist that West
Germany continue to contribute
toward the cost of their forces
in Germany until Bonn's defense
spending becomes comparable to
that of the other NATO powers.


They maintain that West
Germany has no armed forces,
that it's rearmament program is
a year behind schedule and that
it depends entirely on Allied
forces for protection. For the
year ending May 5 the Germans
are paying $760 million to the
three Allies.


West German leaders are di-
vided over the issue.

fer has publicly rejected the
Allied claims, asserting his gov
ernment'S defense contribution
already sis taxing the country's
resources to the utmost"

Brentano and Economic Minister
Ludwig Erhard are reliably re-
ported to favor a compromise.
Mr.. Erhard has said solution
satisfactory to both sides can
be reached.


The German payment takes
care Of such items as wages of
German labor used by the Allied
forces. maintenance of property,
rents of requisitioned houses and
maneuver damages. The Allies
pay and equip their own troops.

say that he was talking politics.

A 26-year-old Seat Pleasant

Thornberry kept her on the phone

address.


She hung up only when she

Pics. John Stout and Robert
Baeschlin approaching the front
of her apartment building in

street.

to talk to the woman a few min
utes before she unlocked her
second-fioor apartment door and
backed off into the kitchen, with
q safety razor blade clutched in
one hand.


II saw some instant coffee on
the table and asked her to make
us some, so maybe we could dis
tract her." Pfc. Baeschlin said.


"She put the blade in her
mouth, declared she'd never turn
her back on any cops. and made
the coffee"


The woman then threatened
to kill herself right away if the
policemen did not close the door
to her husbands bedroom. The
officers complied. and the hus-
band slept through the entire
incident.

ton and coffee drinking, the trio

hair. 1t was down to his shoul-
.ders before he was captured.

peace with President Diem and
brought their men into the gov
eminent army a year ago, but

western part of South Wet Nam

government forces. President
Diem's army finally launched an
about drive in the western
marshes. scattered the rebel
force and captured Gen. Bacut.


His hair cut, he was sentenced
to death in three separate trials
for armed rebellion. treason,
murder, arson and kidnapping

rejected his plea for clemency.

NEW YORK. How good are seat

Answers to these questions, of

new research. Scientists, State

highway is the clinic.


Early findings from automotive

cate the new safety features are
paying on. Meanwhile, still more

1857 models-perhaps including

dashboards less likely to cause in
juries.


These are all part of q new

The premise is this: If an unex-
pected accident does happen even
to expert drivers like you, what
can be done inside the car to re-
duce the chance of death or injury?
Can kind of safety vaccine be
devised against the split-second
exposure to an accident?


A basic approach is to prevent
accidents in the first place, to con-
troll the accident virus.


In that line are old and new
campaigns to reduce speeds, halt
drunken driving, train better driv-
ers. enforce laws, build better high
ways for faSt-expanding traffic,
tighten licensing to weed out in
competent and dangerous drivers,
require periodic exams and even
medical checkups, stress the hor-
ror Of highway deaths, train more
doctors more skillfully in treating
crash injuries and many other
proposals.


The safety devices built into the
car itself are intended to supple
ment these efforts.

street parade provided tantalizing
glimpse of the delights ahead. The
boy had to come early to get spot

times sun. He'd stay there for

nostrils drew in the sweet scent of

Thunder and Blazes." The gnaw-

Many of the indicators still
spelled boom.


Government experts said the
latest figures on employment

average of prices on 80 leading industrial
stocks was down 31.89 points. On that one
day the value of all stocks listed on the
New York Exchange dropped by $14 bill
lion-compared with loss of SIC billion
for the entire month of October, 1929,
remembered for the big crash that pre-
coded four years of depression. Between
last September and April, however, the
market not only recovered but reached a
new peak from which it was dislodged
only when signs of business showdown
showed up this spring When the Presi-
dent was reported i'll on Friday, June 8,
the same average dropped only ~ points.
Within few days it had regained this
loss and had advanced further.


Traditionally the market rises in the
summertime, but presidential election
years have provided most of the excep-
tons to that rule. Wall Street dislikes
uncertainty, but has an almost uncanny
ability to measure at least the economic
and political news in advance. Its
recorded temperature" will be worth
watching for the next few months.

President Eisenhower's proposal to
link the social security and civil service
annuity programs would increase materi-
ally the benefits which Federal employees
receive upon retirement. It is surprising,
therefore, that there should be such Wig
orous opposition to the plan from unions
representing the potential beneflciaries.


The organized opposition developed
not long after legislative advisory conn
mittee, headed by H. Eliot Kaplan, nation
ally known civil service authority, recon-
mended two years ago that social security
supplement the regular annuity system.
Other members of the committee were
Treasury Secretary Humphrey, Defense
Secretary Wilson, Civil Service Commits
sion Chairman Young, Budget Director
Hughes and Federal Reserve Chairman
Martin. President Eisenhower, in for
warding the committees report to Con-
gress, gave the plan his blessing. In the
face Of mounting criticism from employees
unions, however, the administration re-
Trained from urging legislative action
until a few days ago. Apparently It Is
prepared now to put its full weight be-
hind the revised program, despite hear
ings being held on bills preferred by the
unions.


The unions have expressed fears that
the plan to bring Government workers
partly under social security and partly
under the civil service retirement system
is step toward swallowing up" the
latter into the social security program.
The employees want their own security
program, presumably on the theory that
they stand to gain more-both now and
In the future. But the administration
denies any intent to do away with the
present program. The Kaplan commit
tees idea was to supplement present civil
service coverage in such way as to assure
Federal employees who leave the Govern
ment of social security benefits not now
open to them. The Kaplan plan not only
would give former civil service workers
this extra privilege but, Chairman Young
points out, would raise retirement benefits
by about per cent. Furthermore, sur
vivor and disability payments would be
increased. Federal employees ought to
inform themselves fully on the advan-
tages Of the expanded program before
rejecting 1t in favor of something else.
For an extended fight in Congress over
retirement legislation might well result
in no new program at all.

Britain'S island colonies in the Carlb-
bean area have taken another step toward
self-government and independence within
the Commonwealth. After fortnight of
conferences with the Colonial once in
London, delegates from Ave Of the West
Indian colonial Observation-Disclosures,
Trinidad Tobago, the Barbados, the Lee
wards and the Windwards-have agreed
upon a formula for setting up Federal
government and electing Federal legis-
lature before March 81. 1853.


1t is formula, however, that lecves
much yet to be done before an effective
indignation of British dependencies In the
area can evolve into single, strong po-
litical entity. The British Virgin Islands.
British Guiana and British Honduras, for
example, were represented at the London
conferences but are not parties to the
agreement. All may join later but no
commitment has been made. Bermuda
and the Bahamas. not far distant, are
remaining completely aloof-at least for
the time being. And even among those
who signed the agreement numerous
questions were left for later settlement
including the location of the Federal
capital The historic problem of local
rights was recognized In the limitations
laid down for Federal taxing powers and
for appointments by a Federal Governor
General to the upper branch Of the Legis-
lature The lower branch will be elected
on proportionate population basis.


Still. the agreement alone is mark
of progress. The islands have mutual
interests as well as mutual problems
both economic and social. Bringing them
closer together politically should make
easier the resolution of these interests
and problems The federation idea for
these island colonies has had Conserva-
tive Party support in Britain since the
end of World War II, one Of It's first
advocates being Prime Minister Churchill.
The plan was dormant during the Labor
Party administration and was revived
only when the Conservatives returned to
power. There Is promise now that 1t will
lead eventually to another respected
membership in the Commonwealth.

nacles to boat hull. One touch

finally reached shore long after
the herd.

ment. Some Is cowboys, all
members of the department. ride
herd on the ponies. But while

for only once a year, the men
ride their own horses Western
style year-round.

the towns main street to the
corral on the fireman-sponsored
carnival grounds to await today's

text:
Findings Of the Coast Guard In the
disastrous sinking of the pleasure ship
Levin j. Marvel in Chesapeake Bay last
August certainly warrant vigorous prose-
cution of those held to be responsible for
the tragedy Even more important than
the proposed criminal proceedings, how
ever, is the Coast Guard recommendation
that it be given authority to license and
inspect such vessels in the future. It is
hard to understand why such authority
is lacking under existing marine-safetv
regulations


The Marvel was not private cruise
ship. She was an old wooden sailing
craft used in carrying passengers for hire.
On her last trip % passengers and four
crewmen were aboard her. The passen-
gers presumably supposed that the vessel
had been approved by the Coast Guard
for public cruises. In fact, according to
the investigators. the ships owner had
implied in misleading" advertisements
that the ship met safety standards"
Actually, no such Standards" for craft
like the Marvel exist-and, because she
was without power propulsion, the Coast
Guard had no jurisdiction over her. So
the Marvel with her unsuspecting pas
sengers sailed from Annapolis in the face
of storm warnings, continued her cruise
despite hurricane alert and finally
foundered at anchor off Fairhaven, Mary
land, with loss of IA passengers. The
board Of inquiry found that the hull,
launched In 1891, was unseaworthy and
the ship lacked proper lifesaving equip
ment.


While present maritime laws ex-
empted the Marvel from inspection, there
are criminal laws covering ship opera
lions that endanger lives. The Coast
Guard has asked the Department of
Justice to prosecute John Meckling, owner
and skipper Of the Inflated vessel, under
those laws Meanwhile, Congress should
heed promptly the plea of the Coast
Guard for full authority to protect the
public against other tragedies of the
Marvel sort. The glaring loophole in
the maritime. safety laws through which
the Marvel sailed to her doom should be
closed without further delay.

COLUMBUS. Ohio, July 5 (P). !
"A petite, 32-year-old wife of
an Air Force major told sheriff's
deputies today she stabbed her
elderly landlord and his wife to
death when her check forgery
scheme backfired.


Deputies said Mrs. Blanche |
Jacobs, mother of three, spent |
three days trying to conceal the
deaths of her CLOSE" friends,
then told her husband, who took
her to police. Mrs. Jacobs walked
into police headquarters last
night and announced, Il want |
to report a double murder"
police said.


She was accompanied by her
husband. Maj. Eugene w. Jacobs,
IS. who said he had doubted the
bizarre story she blurted out to
him some time earlier.


Authorities checked and found |
the bodies of Andrew j. Robin
son, IA. and his wife, Maude, 70.
side by side in the bathroom of
their suburban Groveport home.
Their bodies showed multiple |
stab wounds.


1t. Ellsworth P. Beck of the
Franklin County sheriff's Office Il
said Mrs. Jacobs gave him
statement admitting she killed
the couple last Monday when
they learned she had forged a
check against Mrs. RobinSon's
bank account. That check and
two others forged by Mrs. Jacobs
totaled $1,149, 1t. Beck said.


Mrs. Jacobs lived next door
to the RobinsonS. Maj. Jacobs,
who is stationed at nearby Lock-
bourne Air Force Base. described
the RobinsonS as very close"
friends.


Cleaned up After Killing


Mrs. Jacobs sobbed intermit-
tently as she told how she
cleaned up the blood-spattered
Robinson home the day after
the killings and dragged the
bodies into the bathroom, 1t.
Beck said.


The lieutenant said Mrs Jacobs
tried to give neighbors the i'm
preston that the RobinSons had
left town. When she realized she
couldn't continue to conceal
what had happened. she told her
husband, 1t. Beck added.


Maj. Jacobs was near collapse
when police told him they had
found the bodies.


The authenticated mother was
held in county Jail for investi-
cation. No charges have been
filed.


This is the story. 1t. Beck
said, that she told of the killings:


She received a call from Mr..
Robinson Monday, asking her to
explain check for about $500
which she had signed in Mrs.
Robinson's name. The other two
forged checks apparently had
not come back from the bank,
1t. Beck said.


Mrs. Jacobs made three or
four visits to the Robinson home
that day. On the last visit Mrs.
Jacobs found Mrs. Robinson pre-
pairing to make a cherry pie in
a second kitchen in the base
ment.


Sort of Went Blank


"They bot to talking about the
check" 1t. Beck said. then
stopped. Mrs. Jacobs said things
sort of went blank and she next
found herself with rolling pin
in her hand. She hit Mrs. Robin
son over the head several times
she doesn't remember how many
and the woman fell to the floor.


About this time. Robinson
came down the basement steps
and Mrs. Jacobs ran past him
into the first floor kitchen and
got a large knife. She ran back
to Robinson and began slashing
him. They fought up the steps.
Robinson collapsed in the first
floor kitchen.


Mrs. Jacobs turned around
and saw Mrs. Robinson, who had
got up from the floor. come up
the steps and go out into the
garage. Mrs. Jacobs ran after
Mrs. Robinson, pulled her back
into the kitchen and stabbed her
numerous times"


1t. Beck said Mrs. Jacobs lad
received a five-year suspended
sentence in Shreveport, La. in
1854, for forging Government
bonds. He said the major has
taken their children, Mike. IL;
Sam, 10, and Belinda, 7, to his
mothers home in San Antonio.
Tex, and promised to return.

the project during the past two years.

lating tangle of red tape, conflicting views

wreck the whole program. But the diff
eulties gradually have been overcome, one
by one For example, the Smithsonian
Institutions air museum, which would

appropriate location. And problems in
volving the inner belt road, land use,
types of development and other matters
have been worked out in commendable
spirit of compromise and joint determi-
nation to get on with the big undertaking.


There are still many planning details
to be settled, but all familiar with the
project are optimistic over eventual
agreement among everybody concerned.

some of the minor details at its March
meeting Final approval of all aspects
of the plan will have to come from the
District Commissioners, after public hear
ings. Once the District formally has
given the go sign, the S96-million re-
building enterprise-the most extensive
ever tried here-can begin. The South
west ace-lifting, with urban redevelop-
ment planned for other rundown parts
of Washington, will give the Nations
Capital a rejuvenating shot in the arm
that should have lasting beneflts-eco-
nomically as well as esthetically.

laration providing independence

eral weeks by Spanish officials

LONDON, May IA (R.-Prime
Minister Eden mapped govern
ment strategy for tonight's
showdown parliament session on
his handling Of the strange case
of the missing British frogman
and the Soviet warships.


Sir Anthony was headed for a
sharp grilling in the House of
Commons debate.


Angry leaders Of the labor OPP
position want to know just what
retired naval diver Lionel Crabb
"a World War II hero-was
doing in the icy waters of Ports
mouth harbor near the Russian
warships that brought Premier
Bulganin and Party Chief Nikita
Khrushchev to Britain.


When the question first came
up in Commons last week, Sir
Anthony said Comdr. Crabb was
operating without authorize
ton" and that it would not be in
the nations best interests to say
more.


The Russians insist the diver
was spying. The British press
generally has agreed.


Sir Anthony said the retired
naval officer was testing under
water apparatus" and refused
to go into details. In the debate
tonight, Laborite legislators
hoped to force him into supply
ing the details.


Comdr. Crabb was seen swim
ming near the Soviet cruiser
Ordzhonikidze. and two accom-
panying vessels on April 49,
the day after the Russian party
arrived in Britain.


He has not been seen since.
The admiralty said he was pre-
sumed dead" but didn't explain
why that was presumed.


The British said in a note they
deeply regret" the whole affair
and obviously hope the Kremlin
will let it drop.


1t appeared that Sir Anthony
could tell all. breaking the case
wide open. Or he could risk a
big loss of prestige rather than
disclose details of a secret serv-
ice cloak and dagger operation
on which Comdr. Crabb might
have been working.


Sir Anthony cut short a week.

and slim became social grace.

sidered unforgiveable in the
haut monde. Then, when Pres
ident EiSenhower's heart at
tack became the subject of
international discussion, the
possible consequences of too
much weight came to be known

France. no longer was it re-
garded as frivolous snobbery

avenue area will come before
the House District Committee

early next week.


This was indicated today after
Ia District subcommittee agreed
to recommend a bridge instead
of tunnel for the long-planned
crossing. Subcommittee Chair
man Davis. Democrat Of Georgia,
said his unit had agreed on q
Isix-lane bridge with draw span,
similar to the draw in the Ar
Ilington Memorial Bridge.

structure, the Davis subcommit-
tee voted to accept Senate
passed bill for the bridge with
two important amendments.

prepared for action by the full
District Committee, would spec
ify that the span should be six
lanes, and should have the draw
span.


Conference May Result


If the District Committee and
the House itself should approve
the Senate bill with these two
amendments. the legislation
would go back to the Senate.
The Senate then could either
accept the House amendments
and send the measure to the
White House or could ask for a
conference with the House over
the differences.


Representative Davis expressed
hope that both the District
COMMITTEES and the House itself
would approve the amended
Senate bill.


Could Start Behring'S


The District now has available
SO million to proceed with the
construction. An additional 50
million has been approved by
Congress in the Districts annual
appropriation bill now awaiting
President Eisenhower's signature.


If Congress approves the new
bridge bill for six lanes and a
draw span, and the President
also approves, District officials
said today they could start the
first actual construction with
borings to determine the under
ground geology of the site.

The cause of honest law enforcement
has been strengthened by the decision of
the United States Court of Appeals up
holding the conviction of two former
Metropolitan Police officers on conspiracy
to-bribe charges. The guilty officers,
former Captain John B. Monroe and for
mer Detective George c. Prather, had
appealed their conviction on technical
grounds. But the appellate tribunal ruled
that the District Court committed no re-
verSible error. In other words, it found
that these suspended policemen-and the
numbers racketeerS with whom they
plotted to bride a gambling squad officer
were given fair trial before the lower
court jury.


The appeal of the convicted officers
was based chiefly on the fact that there
was variance" between the conspiracy
count and the proof presented in District
Court in support of the count. Curiously,
the variance involved not too little evil
dence, but too much. Defense attorneys
pointed out that whereas the count had
to do with only one alleged conspiracy,
the Government produced evidence of
several conSpiracieS. 1t was argued, I'M
der previous court decisions, that this
additional evidence constituted surprise
tactics that put the defense at
disadvantage.


But Appellate Judges Miller, Fahy
and Danaher brushed aside the surprise"
contention with the assertion that 1.-The
scheme of Monroe and Prather extended
to all that was proved respecting the
conspiracy. They were not surprised, nor
were their substantial rights otherwise
prejudced by the alleged variance" The
judges also upheld the use of recorded
evidence against the pair. The unanimous
decision is gratifying to citizens who had
been shocked at revelations of police
corruption and who have backed Chief
Murray in his determined efforts to rid
his force of crooked officers.

A poignant and yet heart

a meeting this week of the Cen
trail Union Missions ministerial
council.


Mrs. Herbert E. Eberhardt, di-
rector of children's work at the
mission, related the incident.


Recently three little girls were
brought to the mission by their
father. They looked underfed
and were poorly dressed. Their
mother had left the small family
and the father wanted to leave
the children temporarily at the
home.


Despite the unhappy circum-
stances, the girls chung to their
father.


why do you have to leave us
here?" they sobbed.


The haraSsed man was look

door to the room opened and a
small 8-year-old girl came

ing. The child was all smiles as
she rushed over to Mrs. Eber-
hardt and flung her arms around
the children's work director

claimed how happy she was to
be back.

scene, the three little girls
stopped crying and became ST.
lent. They watched the 8-year-
ODDS actions intently.


After she left, the three chill

leave without protest.


Apparently, Mrs. Eberhardt
observed, the reactions of the
other child had convinced them
staying at the MISSIONS home
could not be too bad. The three
have been at the home since,
and are doing very well, the d.
rector added.

center in the industrial city of

portedly rushed into the city

Surveys among Hungarian
refugees indicate that So per
cent of them listened to West
ern radio broadcasts of news and

The Austrian Institute for
Market and Opinion Research
posed this question to the Hun
garians:


when you were in Hungary

broadasts OF Western radio sta
tionS?"


Eighty-two per cent said. they
listened often, IA per cent said
they listened occasionally. and
only 4 per cent said they did
not listen at all.


Only Reliable Source


Other similar reports of the
unexpected effectiveness of West
ern radio stations have strength
ened the view of many Washing
ton diplomats that the programs,
especially the newscasts. should
be continued and perhaps ex-
panded.


Many refugees have said that
the Western broadcasts provide
people behind the Iron Curtain
with their only reliable source of
news. Official texts Of Western
government statements usually
are not available in the Soviet
satellite countries.


Some critics of the Western
broadcasts have charged that
Radio Free Europe and the Voice
of America incited the Hungarian
revolt. The West German gov
ernment has launched an inves-
tigation Of the broadcasts.


The Austrian survey showed
that agricultural workers and
village inhabitants listened least
to Western broadcasts. The
highest percentages Of coverage
were among city workers.


Among the SO per cent of the
Hungarian refugees who said
they had listended often or oc-
casionally to Western programs.
70 per cent said they tuned in
Radio Free Europe most fire.
quently: 30 per cent named

British stations as their first
choice; 20 per cent said they
listened most frequently to
American stations. Nine per
cent said they listened to all
stations they could locate.


Multiple Answers


The percentages add up to
more than 100 per cent, the Aus
trian research institute explains
because some refugees gave
|''multiple answers" The figures
signify. however. the relative
popularity of the various West
ern broadcastS.


The Hungarians coming across
the Austrian border were also
asked what they thought the
Western nations should have
done to help the cause of the
revolution.


Twenty-three per cent said
they thought United Nations
police force should have been
sent; another % per cent said
diplomatic negotiations with
Russia should have been ini-
tiated Immediately; 20 per cent
favored delivering arms to the
freedom fighters; 10 per cent
said other kinds of military aid
should have been sent.


Only IL per cent would have
advocated a war against the
Soviet Union. Nine per cent sug-
gested breaking of diplomatic
relations with Russia. Seven per
cent said an economic boycott
of the Soviet Union should have
been attempted. Multiple an
swers again account for the
more than 100 per cent total, the
Austrian institute notes.

GLENN MILLER ORCHESTRA - RAY MCKINLEY


It's good news to report that the Glenn Miller
orchestra, under the direction of Ray Mckinley,
will be appearing at the Totem Pole in Auburndale
next Wednesday


It was almost foregone conclusion that Ray
McKinley's talents and Glenn Miller's music should
ultimately get together again. Rays friendship with
and admiration for Glenn goes back almost rs
years!


In the early thirties Ray came to Chicago.
Glenn starting his career as arranger and
trombonist for Ben Polack Ray often "sat in" with
Pollacks band. Glenn liked the way Ray played
and Ray impressed with Glenns imaginative
and fine writing. They became very close friends
and remained so through the years.


When Glenn left Pollack to organize a band
for Smith Be,lew, he chose Ray as drummer. The
band did well but not nearly as well as the Dorsey
Brothers, whose band Glenn also organized and
wrote Hor McKinley's drumming and MillerS writ
ing soon made it the top band Of it's day.


Glenn fast becoming the country's best
known and most sought after organizer, arranger
and trombonst. Ray Noble came over from England
and asked Glenn to organize an American band
for him. Glenn left the DorseyS, Mckinley stayed
on, later joining Jimmy DorSeys band when the
brothers split


The Ray Noble orchestra, with Glenn's arrange
ments, became top-notch outfit. Glenn then be-
gan to think about forming his own band and did
in 1887. 1t wasn't until the Spring of '39 that it
really caught the publics fancy For the next 8
years, Glenn Miller reigned as Americas number





of the greatest popular band of aH-tme


Glenn Miller featured liquid reeds with a unique
clarinet lead "ooh wah" brass, romantic ballads
swing tunes and novelties. He went into the Army
in October ~ as Captain. After his AAF band
played all over the U. S. they went overseas Glenn
had questioned his old civilian buddy now Sgt Ray
Mckinley. Glenn suggested to Ray in New Haven
1874 that Ray work up march-tempo arrangements
on top pop favorites That's where "St: Louis Blues
March" jersey Bounce March, and similar items
originated


In Europe they broadcasted over BIC, AFN
made records and transcriptionS and played for
CTS and tcyalty Rays vocals, drumming and per-
Sonality were of the reasons for their success


After Millers tragic disappearance on a flight
over the English Channel (Dec 44) it was Ray
who took over and kept the Miller music and spirit
going Mckinley was later discharged formed his
own band, got stomach virus and temporarily gave
up his loved music He went back to Texas as a
disc jockey Later he organized a band to play
dates on weekendS His love for music never Waned


His love for the Glenn Miller music never died
either The Glenn Miller Story made Americans re-
Miller estate and top agent Willard Alexander de-
cided to do something about it. They contacted
Mckinley, Glenns logical successor. They gave him
backing, rights to all the original Glenn Miller
rangements


This brought together again the combination
that thrilled millions both sides of the Atlantic
And now, because OF Rays respect and admiration
for Glenn and his music, you'll be able to hear
once more - live - the Glenn Miller orchestra at
the beautiful Totem Pole in Auburndale Mass.

Not much more than a year ago,
there was great hullabaloo in this
country over the Salk vaccine. Amid
cries of emergency" and "crisis," there
were solemn warnings that the wondrous
new antipolio weapon was being turned
out far too slowly and would remain
scarce for long time to come unless the
Government moved in with big stick to
beat private enterprise into faster pro-
duction. Indeed, there were some indi-
viduals and groups who filled the air with
Strident demands for an exceedingly
drastic Federal law to expedite the vac
cine'S manufacture, control its distribu-
ton, and severely punish BLACK market
GERS" supposedly making all sorts Of vile
profit out Of the temporary shortage.


The monumental nonsense inherent
in all this became abundantly clear
months ago, and now 1t has been under
scored by Marion B. Folsom, Health, Edu-
cation and Welfare Secretary. For the
fact is, as Mr.. Folsom has declared to the
National Press Club, that large supplies
Of the Salk vaccine are piled up in ware
houses and sitting unused on drugstore
shelves in an abundance that mocks the
alarmist talk Of the past about the threat
OF critical long-term scarcity. Actually,
the supplies are plentiful enough TO meet
the needs Of every American child and
young adult. But there appears to be
public apathy toward getting inoculated.
and one has reason to wonder-as Mr.
Folsom has wondered-why no shouting
is being done about this by those very
same people who last year were saying
so much, so loudly. about terrible pro-
spective shortage and the need for sweep
ing Federal action, which. wisely, was
never taken.

This sort of -and-take has
